opening.headline: We explore how to combine pricing strategies when dealing with services that involve continuous, sudden spikes, and large-scale nighttime operations, and how to evaluate both total cost and risk together.
body: There are always a steady stream of requests, sudden spikes at specific times, and large batch jobs running overnight within a single service. Processing all calls on a pay-per-use basis incurs costs during baseline loads and reaches limits during peak times. Conversely, reserving all capacity leads to unnecessary expenses during idle periods and overnight batch operations.

In this class, we compare the cost structures of spot, reservation, priority, Flex, and batch instances in a single overview, focusing on appropriate traffic patterns. We then learn the framework for calculating total costs and the perspective of risk diversification, compare the monthly costs and risks of three different configurations, and explain the design rationale for a combination that uses reservations, overage spot pricing, and batch instances together.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Billing method suitability can be compared by traffic type.
The total cost and risk of the proposal can be evaluated together.

screens.title: A combination of charging rates for ongoing, sudden spikes, and large-scale nighttime operations
screens.lead: First, take a look at a scenario where different types of traffic are mixed within a single service. The diagram divides the daily usage into three segments.

visual.alt: A daily usage graph divided into three segments—continuous baseline load, weekday morning spike, and overnight bulk operations—color-coded for distinction.

paragraphs: Take an internal document analysis service as an example. During off-peak hours, a steady level of employee inquiries continues to come in. On Monday mornings, requests accumulate suddenly. And overnight, large-scale processing tasks analyze the documents accumulated during the previous day.

If all three are handled under a pay-as-you-go model, prices are reduced during baseline loads, but errors occur when demand spikes and capacity is reached. Conversely, if all are pre-booked to match peak demand, fixed charges apply during idle periods and overnight operations as well. Since each billing method has different cost structures and risks, unifying them results in losses somewhere.
The approach involves using different means tailored to the shape of traffic, segmented by interval. This lesson discusses the criteria used to determine such combinations.

callout.label: Questions to be answered in this class
callout.text: How should pricing mechanisms be combined to match traffic patterns, and how should we evaluate whether such a combination is effective?

screens.outro: First, let's review the current approach of our service.

screens.title: Think about whether only one billing method is being used currently.
screens.lead: First, think through each question on your own before selecting an answer. The instructor's thoughts will then be organized and presented. No answers are submitted.

items.prompt: Are you currently processing all calls under the same billing method?
items.answer: If unified across all segments, management becomes simple, but waste occurs per segment. In certain segments, reservations are more appropriate, while in others where delays are allowed, placement or Flex is better suited.

items.prompt: Do you know the steady request level maintained throughout the day?
items.answer: This level represents the baseline load and serves as the basis for reservations. Since you need to find a level that is consistently exceeded—rather than just the average—you should plot the hourly usage distribution once.

items.prompt: Isn't there a bulk operation that allows for delays and is not using the standard path?
items.answer: When standard paths are used for tasks whose results are needed later, such as night-time analysis or end-of-month reports, real-time limits are also consumed while performing the same work at standard cost. Candidates for batch or Flex processing.

items.prompt: Do you have a response plan when the limit is reached?
items.answer: Without a response plan, the surge phase will directly become a service outage. You must proactively establish either a path to allow excess reservations beyond capacity to flow through a volume-based mechanism or a request pathway to increase limits.

screens.outro: Now I will check one by one which cost structure each billing method has.

screens.title: Cost structure and suitability for traffic of billing mechanisms
screens.lead: The following flashcard describes traffic matching the cost structures of five funding methods. Select the card to flip it. Use the right arrow to advance to the next card.

cards.back: You only pay for what you use, and there is no commitment. Costs are low and scalability is easy during periods of low usage. However, there is a risk of reaching capacity limits during peak times, and capacity is not guaranteed. This model is suitable for use cases with irregular usage patterns or those that benefit from excess capacity.

This includes Google's Provisioned Throughput and OpenAI's Reserved Tier. With throughput secured at a fixed cost, there is no cost even when usage is low. It is suitable when a consistent high baseline load and a consistent user experience with predictable costs are required. OpenAI Reserved Tier does not apply to Batch or Flex.

Pays a premium price for low latency and high reliability. Compared to standard offerings, Gemini's documentation shows a 75% to 100% higher cost. The cost should only be applied to core user-facing calls where latency is critical.

While offering a 50% discount compared to standard, the delay is variable and availability is at best-effort level. Since it's a synchronous call that returns a response immediately, it's not urgent, but the call structure fits well with tasks we don't want to refactor.

All three providers utilize asynchronous processing to reduce costs by 50%. The target completion time is within 24 hours, and some providers also use separate rate limit pools. Results are aligned with subsequent work that is needed later, such as large-scale overnight tasks.

screens.outro: Now that we understand the characteristics by category, let's establish a framework for evaluating the strengths and weaknesses of combinations.

screens.title: Framework for Total Cost Comparison and Risk Diversification
screens.lead: The following is an example of a hypothetical index used to calculate the total cost and risk of a portfolio. Refer to the explanation on the right to verify the calculation order and how to read the risk.

data.code:
Assumption: Monthly cost calculated at a volumetric fixed price = 100 (hypothetical index)
  Base load segment 40 + Surge segment 20 + Night heavy load segment 40
Assumption: It is assumed that reservation throughput processes 25% less than the actual volume at the list price (hypothetical)
Assumption: The batch costs 50% of the list price.

[Proposal A] Full quantity-based pricing
  Base 40 + Spike 20 + Nighttime 40 = 100

[Proposal C] Reservation + Limited Quantity (excess portion) + Scheduling
  Basic load -> Reserved          40 x 0.75 = 30
  Surge section -> Fixed dosage        20 x 1.00 = 20
  Night bulk -> Dispatch          40 x 0.50 = 20
  Monthly cost index = 70

Risk Assessment
  Credit Risk: Basic burden is reserved, hence low.
  Delay risk: Due to the batched large-scale deployment during nighttime (up to 24 hours), it is intermediate.
  Flexibility: The base load during the reservation period is fixed.

notes.note: This is an assumption to calculate total costs by segments. In reality, costs should be broken down by service and tier, and the respective pricing values from each provider's price list should be used. The numbers here are merely hypothetical indices for illustrative purposes.
This is the base scenario A. All segments are calculated at full price, resulting in an index of 100. The risk of reaching the limit is highest, while the risk of delay is low, and scaling is easy.

Basic load is reserved, peak demand is metered, and nighttime bulk usage is scheduled. The total cost is derived by summing up costs per interval. If any interval's assumption is incorrect, the total cost will differ, so it is important to establish the assumptions first.

Cost alone is not sufficient to determine a combination. You must also consider capacity risk, delay risk, and flexibility together. Over-reserving leads to wasted fixed costs, while under-reserving increases excess costs and capacity risk. Relying solely on a single supplier or single resource amplifies the impact of outages or capacity changes.

screens.outro: Since we've verified the template, let's compare the monthly costs and risks across the three combination options in a table.

screens.title: Cost and risk comparison of the three proposal plans per month
screens.lead: The numbers in the table are hypothetical indices provided for illustrative purposes, with the total quantity-based price set to 100. Please do not read only the cost column; also review the risk column.

data.caption: Comparison of three combination plans (virtual index)
data.notes: C's low cost is due to reserving basic capacity and shifting bulk off-peak workloads into scheduled batches, resulting in a reduction of approximately 50%. However, this comes with an increased risk of delay. B reserves capacity sufficiently to cover peak demand, including fixed costs during idle periods, making it difficult to scale during the contract period, and costs remain unchanged even if traffic decreases after reservation. A is the most flexible option but carries a high risk of reaching capacity limits during peak times. Whether one option is better depends on whether cost or risk is prioritized. For critical calls that users are waiting on, some Priority or Fast options can be applied, in which case C's cost increases above the table value. When reviewing the table, first identify the lowest-cost option in the cost column, then check the risk column to understand the risk associated with that option. Finally, evaluate whether you can bear that risk and whether mitigation measures are available—this provides the basis for selecting a suitable combination.

screens.outro: In the table, C appears to be well-balanced. I will now provide a step-by-step explanation of the design rationale.

screens.title: Explanation: Design rationale for reservation + limited quantity (excess portion) + batch combination
screens.lead: The instructor breaks down the scenario step by step. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

steps.title: Divide the traffic into three segments
steps.body: The service demand is steady and predictable, surges on Mondays morning, and involves large-scale analysis during nighttime hours. Since the waiting time and usage patterns vary by interval, different measures are implemented for each interval.

steps.title: Basic provisioning is reserved.
steps.body: We secure capacity up to the base load through reserved throughput. This ensures stable cost and performance, reducing concerns about reaching limits. By operating at a level that consistently exceeds peak demand, we avoid unnecessary downtime.

steps.title: Apply fast priority only to delayed-sensitive calls.
steps.body: The core call that the user is waiting for examines Priority or Fast settings. However, this applies only to calls that are sensitive to latency, not to all calls. Due to the premium pricing, expanding the scope would eliminate the cost savings. First, determine what percentage of calls are latency-sensitive.

steps.title: Night-time bulk analysis is scheduled as a batch job.
steps.body: Nightly analysis is moved to batch processing, achieving approximately a 50% reduction in cost. Verify whether the target completion time is within 24 hours and whether the logic for retrieving results is in place. Also define how the process will be rehandled if the batch fails or expires.

steps.title: The excess is discharged according to a fixed quantity.
steps.body: Surges beyond reservation are handled on a volume-based basis. Additional capacity can be provisioned if available and within limits, allowing requests to be fulfilled, though the cost in this tier is fixed. The volume-based tier may also reach its limit, so usage tier and limit escalation requests should be reviewed.

steps.title: Review and adjust monthly
steps.body: Monthly review of reservation utilization, batch completion time, and proportional allocation adjusts the ratios accordingly. Since the shape of traffic changes, the optimal configuration also changes, so the settings are never final. The review results are directly reflected in the reservation size and batch selection for the following month.

screens.outro: Next, we will examine how to reduce the risk of this combination.

screens.title: Explanation: How to reduce the risk of a portfolio
screens.lead: When you select a risk, the mitigation methods recommended by the instructor appear. Read through and consider which risk is most relevant to our service.

items.title: Reservation overcapacity risk
items.body: Reserving large resources poses a risk of underutilization. Set the baseline load based on the minimum usage interval, and gradually increase it based on observed usage. Also verify whether the scale can be adjusted again when the reservation period ends.

items.title: Reservation shortage risk
items.body: With a small reservation, there is a risk of exceeding capacity. Monitor excess costs and proximity to limits, and review additional reservations or limit increases if necessary.

items.title: Risk of misusing delay tolerance level
items.body: Delays in Flex or batch processing pose a risk to user experience. Establish rules that set a completion deadline and allow fallback to a standard path. Flex relies on availability to the best of its efforts, making fallback particularly important.

items.title: Vendor dependency risk
items.body: Relying on a single supplier or a single path can result in significant disruptions or changes in capacity limits. Ensure gateway design includes multiple suppliers for core paths.

items.title: Relaxation from an operational perspective
items.body: From the operational excellence perspective of Well-Architected, it recommends establishing metrics, alerts, and regular reviews to continuously tune the system. From the cost optimization perspective, it suggests defining and measuring cost versus outcomes, and implementing expenditure controls. The effectiveness of these practices is verified through measurement. Without metrics, simply changing configurations cannot determine whether costs have decreased or risks have increased.

screens.outro: Now I will summarize the previous content into a single reference point.

screens.title: Summary: Combinations match the traffic pattern.
screens.lead: Summarize the content discussed so far. Please read the following paragraphs in sequence.

paragraphs: The starting point for billing is the shape of traffic. The basic baseline is reservations; delay-sensitive calls are handled with Priority or Fast; large-scale asynchronous workloads are batched; and the remainder of spikes are managed on a pay-per-use basis. This is the fundamental framework presented in this course.

When evaluating a combination, total cost and risk are considered together. Total cost is the sum of costs across segments, and risk includes over-reservation and under-reservation, misusage of delay grades, and supplier dependency. Looking only at cost may overlook delay risks. For example, if night-time bulk operations are shifted to a schedule to reduce costs, it is necessary to also assess whether the increased delay risk is acceptable.

Allocation is not a one-time setting. It must be regularly reviewed and adjusted for metrics such as reservation utilization, batch completion time, and volume-based proportion, especially when traffic changes. This ongoing cycle ensures that allocation evolves alongside the service. This is the core conclusion of this course.

glossary.def: The service is receiving requests with different shapes—such as continuous, sudden spikes, and large-scale asynchronous requests—mixed together.
This is a design that divides reservation, limited quantity, priority level, Flex, and scheduling by traffic intervals.
This involves comparing the monthly cost totals and risks of each portfolio option under the same framework.
An approach that reduces limits, delays, over- and under-reservation, and supplier dependency through various means.

misconceptions.myth: The cheapest single option is optimal.
misconceptions.fact: If a single approach is used universally, delays and capacity risks increase, potentially raising total costs. The appropriate approach varies by traffic segment.

misconceptions.myth: Reservations should be as large as peak demand.
misconceptions.fact: Excess beyond reservation is handled on a volumetric basis, but this does not guarantee adherence to volumetric limits or availability. It is typical to scale according to baseline load.

misconceptions.myth: A combination once set is final.
misconceptions.fact: When traffic patterns change, the optimal configuration also changes. You must continuously adjust based on usage metrics.

closing.lead: Summarizes the key points of this class.
points: The combination adapts to the traffic pattern.
Basic provisioning is reserved; delay-sensitive calls are handled with Priority or Fast, bulk asynchronous operations are scheduled, and surges are managed on a throttled basis.
The total cost is the sum of costs per segment and must be read in conjunction with the risk exposure.
The consortium continuously adjusts through usage checks.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: What approaches are appropriate for our service's steady, spike, and high-volume scenarios?

title: Designing pricing combinations for mixed traffic

checks.q: In the comparison table, the monthly cost index of combination C (reservation + quantity-based (overage) + allocation) is approximately 70, the lowest. Why is this the case?
options: This is because all calls were shifted to Priority, improving processing efficiency.
The reservation size is adjusted to the peak maximum value, which causes the variable usage to disappear.
Basic provisioning is reserved, and batch processing for nighttime heavy workloads has been shifted, resulting in a reduction of approximately 50%.
The credit risk has increased, causing the actual usage to decrease.
checks.explain: We stabilized the on-demand workload through reservations and offloaded large, delay-tolerant jobs to batch processing, achieving cost reductions. However, it's also important to note that the delay risk has increased to medium level, and this must be considered alongside cost considerations.

wrong.0: Priority is not a means to reduce costs by charging a premium price.
wrong.1: Reservations matched to peak periods result in fixed costs being incurred even during off-peak times, leading to waste.
wrong.3: The limit risk of the table is low, and the cost difference arises from the pricing mechanism combination, not from reduced usage.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded.

checks.q: Pair the risks of billing combinations with methods to mitigate them.
right: Design the gateway to handle core paths through more than one supplier.
Define completion deadlines and standard path fallback rules for batch and Flex requests.
Start with the base load based on the minimum usage interval and increase it gradually.
Monitors excess costs and proximity to limits, and reviews additional reservations.
checks.explain: Each risk requires a different mitigation approach because it has a different root cause. Start small with reservations and gradually scale up, monitor the excess, include fallbacks for delay levels, and disperse supplier dependencies through design.
